rationale: The literature supports a broad genotype-phenotype correlation in FDXR-related disorders where residual ferredoxin reductase activity modulates clinical severity. However, the rigid dichotomy proposed in the hypothesis—that biallelic null/truncating variants specifically cause early-infantile encephalopathy and severe microcephaly while hypomorphic missense variants are confined to late-infantile, juvenile, or adult-onset isolated optic atrophy and auditory neuropathy—is directly conflicted by clinical cohorts. Specifically, Yi et al. (2023) demonstrated that patients carrying exclusively biallelic missense variants frequently present in early infancy (within months of birth) with severe congenital amaurosis, nystagmus, and early-onset severe retinal dystrophy rather than mild, late-onset isolated optic atrophy. Furthermore, Pignatti et al. (2024) identified systemic endocrine manifestations (adrenal insufficiency and atypical sexual development / 46,XX DSD) alongside encephalopathy and sensory neuropathy, showing that phenotypic outcomes involve tissue-specific pathways (such as mitochondrial steroidogenesis and iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis) rather than a linear spectrum based purely on variant truncation vs. hypomorphic classification.

evidence.text: Biallelic pathogenic FDXR variants were identified in 11 unrelated probands presenting with severe congenital or early-infantile ocular disease; all 14 variants identified were missense variants. Four patients presented with congenital amaurosis within months of birth with nystagmus, and seven presented in early childhood with early-onset severe retinal dystrophy and severe optic atrophy, conflicting with the claim that missense alleles only cause late-infantile/juvenile/adult isolated optic neuropathy.

evidence.text: In a systematic evaluation of 50 nuclear genes associated with hereditary optic neuropathies across 826 families (including 473 nHON probands), FDXR was identified as one of the top five nuclear causative genes alongside OPA1, WFS1, ACO2, and AFG3L2, causing optic atrophy with or without concurrent retinal degeneration and complex encephalopathy.

conflicts: Patients harboring exclusively missense variants can present with congenital amaurosis and severe retinal dystrophy manifesting in the first months of life (Yi et al., 2023), contradicting the claim that missense alleles cause only late-infantile, juvenile, or adult-onset mild sensory neuropathy/isolated optic atrophy.

The phenotypic spectrum includes severe extra-neurological findings such as primary adrenal insufficiency and disorders of sex development (46,XX DSD) due to disruption of mitochondrial steroidogenesis electron transfer (Pignatti et al., 2024; Miller, 2021), which is not accounted for by a pure neuro-ophthalmic/encephalopathy severity scale.

new_directions.question_text: Do specific missense variants in the NADPH- vs. FAD-binding domains of FDXR selectively impair mitochondrial CYP-mediated steroidogenesis versus Fe-S cluster biogenesis in patient-derived models?
new_directions.rationale: Differentiating between the two distinct mitochondrial electron-transfer roles of FDXR (Fe-S cluster biogenesis affecting respiratory complexes vs. electron delivery to CYP11A1/steroidogenic enzymes) could clarify why some patients develop early adrenal insufficiency and DSD while others exhibit purely oculoneuropathic features.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic frequency of concurrent retinal dystrophy and electroretinographic abnormalities in FDXR patients compared to other primary mitochondrial optic neuropathies (OPA1, ACO2)?
new_directions.rationale: Yi et al. (2023) and Zheng et al. (2025) note prominent retinal vessel attenuation and retinal degeneration alongside optic atrophy, which may provide a key discriminating biomarker from OPA1-associated dominant optic atrophy.
